doc.title: Richard Wyands interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Union checks and discovering the hit on a jukebox
summary: He heard 'Don't Go to Strangers' at Minton's and had no royalties from the hit.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: And what did a record date pay back then?
I don’t remember. It’s hard to say.
Would that be a thing where you would go to the union office at some later date—

Right. The union wouldn’t send you a notice that your check, or any checks, were there unless you had so many, like some of the musicians who did recording work every day, but they would call you perhaps, but usually you’d have to call them. And usually, “no, we don’t have anything for you yet, no” and three or four months had gone by it seemed like.
It might be easy to forget who actually owes you.

That’s why I forgot what we played. So one day I was working at Minton’s Playhouse up in Harlem and on a jukebox I heard this record “Don’t Go to Strangers,” and it was Etta Jones. So I said sounds familiar, I thought to myself. Months later, and it was a hit. I didn’t even know it was a hit at the time. I checked it out and sure enough, that was the record I was on. I said wow, a hit. Of course the record company didn’t tell me that, no man.
And it didn’t make any difference what money you were going to make off it anyway, did it?
No there was no money, no royalties, no. Well you know how that goes. They made a lot of money on that record. One of the few hits. That was a million copy hit I guess.
